understanding.summary: sqlparse is a non-validating SQL parser for Python. It lexes SQL into tokens, splits the token stream into statements, optionally groups tokens into a tree (identifiers, parentheses, functions, comparisons, etc.), and can reformat SQL (reindent, case changes, aligned indent, comment stripping, output as Python/PHP snippets). Layout: sqlparse/lexer.py (regex-based tokenizer driven by the SQL_REGEX table in keywords.py), engine/ (FilterStack, StatementSplitter, grouping), sql.py (token and token-list classes: Statement, Identifier, Parenthesis, etc.), filters/ (formatting filters), formatter.py (option validation and filter stack construction), cli.py (sqlformat). The benchmark generates 160 deterministic SELECT/INSERT statements and runs split, format(reindent=True, keyword_case=upper, identifier_case=lower) and parse on each. Time is likely spent in the regex lexer, the many passes of engine/grouping.py over token lists (with repeated index lookups and token_next scans in sql.py), and the reindent filter, which re-walks and mutates the token tree.

workload_notes.20b64e03-4123-46d2-ad21-e15801ceb5e8: Runs benchmarks/bench_sqlparse.py: builds a seeded script of 160 SQL statements (joins, subqueries, CASE, GROUP BY, inserts), then splits it, formats each statement with reindent and case options, parses each and hashes the results.

candidate_modules.reason: Runs many sequential grouping passes over each statement's token list, using recursion and repeated token_next/index lookups; it is likely the main cost of parse and format.
Token and TokenList classes with token_index, token_next_by, flatten and get_* helpers, used heavily by grouping and filters. Linear scans and repeated list operations are hot.
Tokenizer that matches regexes at each position of the input; it runs for every split, format and parse call.
Holds SQL_REGEX and the keyword lookup tables used by the lexer; the regex order and the keyword-matching callbacks affect tokenizing speed.
ReindentFilter walks the statement tree and inserts and removes whitespace tokens, with frequent token_next and index operations; used by the benchmark's format step.
State machine that scans every token to split statements; it runs on every call.
Orchestrates lexing, splitting, grouping and filters as generators for every call.
Contains whitespace-stripping and other filters that format() applies when reindenting.
KeywordCaseFilter and IdentifierCaseFilter process every token when the case options are enabled.
Builds the filter stack from options on each format() call; the order of the filters determines how much work is done.

audited_returned: Build TokenList values incrementally from direct children instead of re-flattening whole subtrees on each group
Fuse the statement splitter's token loop checks into a fast path for ordinary tokens
Skip no-op _group passes in statements lacking the trigger token (precomputed token-type presence check)
Skip lexer regex attempts by caching a first-character dispatch in Lexer.get_tokens
Make imt and token_next_by avoid lambda and generic dispatch overhead in sql.py
Speed up Token.match by avoiding generator and tuple rebuilds
Replace tokens.__contains__ ttype checks in hot paths with identity or precomputed flags

understanding.summary: Tomli is a pure-Python TOML v1.1 parser (optionally compiled with mypyc) that exposes loads(), load() and TOMLDecodeError. The code lives in src/tomli: __init__.py re-exports the API, _parser.py holds the hand-written recursive-descent parser (statement loop, key/value rules, string/array/inline-table parsing, a Flags/NestedDict/Output structure for table bookkeeping), and _re.py has the regexes and converters for numbers, datetimes and local times. The workload is benchmarks/bench_tomli.py, which generates a deterministic 400-table TOML document (escaped and multi-line strings, ints in four bases, floats, dates and times, arrays, inline tables, arrays of tables), parses it 8 times with tomli.loads, and hashes the JSON-dumped result. Run time is dominated by the character-by-character Python loops in _parser.py (skip_chars, string parsing, key parsing, value dispatch), the regex matching and conversion in _re.py, and the per-key flag and namespace checks. The json.dumps hashing in the benchmark adds a small constant overhead. Tests, the toml-test data, the fuzzer and the profiler are not on the hot path.

workload_notes.a8bbdd59-2d59-4098-8ab9-9c5aa96a53ab: Runs benchmarks/bench_tomli.py: builds a seeded 400-table TOML document, parses it 8 times with tomli.loads from src/tomli, JSON-dumps each result into a sha256 digest and prints it.

candidate_modules.reason: Core parser: the loads() statement loop, skip_chars, key_value_rule, parse_key, string parsing (basic, literal, multiline with escapes), parse_value, arrays, inline tables, and the Flags/NestedDict/Output table bookkeeping. Nearly all of the run time is spent here in Python-level per-character loops and dict/set operations.

Regexes and converters for numbers, datetimes and local times (match_to_number, match_to_datetime, match_to_localtime, cached_tz). It is called for every scalar value, so match and conversion overhead adds up.
Workload driver: document generation and json.dumps digesting add a modest fixed cost, but the parse loop is what is being measured.
Thin re-export of the public API; only relevant for import time.
